hmmt-feb-2018-team-01.prompt: In an $n\times n$ square array of $1\times1$ cells, at least one cell is colored pink. Show that you can always divide the square into rectangles along cell borders such that each rectangle contains exactly one pink cell.
hmmt-feb-2018-team-01.answer: Prove the statement for any rectangular array by induction on the number of pink cells, splitting along a grid line that separates two pink cells.

hmmt-feb-2018-team-02.prompt: Is the number $$\left(1+\frac12\right)\left(1+\frac14\right)\left(1+\frac16\right)\cdots\left(1+\frac1{2018}\right)$$ greater than, less than, or equal to $50$?
hmmt-feb-2018-team-02.answer: Less than $50$: its square is less than $2019<50^2$.

hmmt-feb-2018-team-03.prompt:
Michelle has a word with $2^n$ letters, where a word can consist of letters from any alphabet. Michelle performs a *switcheroo* on the word as follows: for each $k=0,1,\dots,n-1$, she switches the first $2^k$ letters of the word with the next $2^k$ letters of the word. For example, for $n=3$, Michelle changes $$ABCDEFGH\to BACDEFGH\to CDBAEFGH\to EFGHCDBA$$ in one switcheroo.

In terms of $n$, what is the minimum positive integer $m$ such that after Michelle performs the switcheroo operation $m$ times on any word of length $2^n$, she will receive her original word?

hmmt-feb-2018-team-04.prompt: In acute triangle $ABC$, let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of the altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ respectively, and let $L$, $M$, and $N$ be the midpoints of $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Lines $DE$ and $NL$ intersect at $X$, lines $DF$ and $LM$ intersect at $Y$, and lines $XY$ and $BC$ intersect at $Z$. Find $\frac{ZB}{ZC}$ in terms of $AB$, $AC$, and $BC$.

hmmt-feb-2018-team-05.prompt: Is it possible for the projection of the set of points $(x,y,z)$ with $0\le x,y,z\le1$ onto some two-dimensional plane to be a simple convex pentagon?
hmmt-feb-2018-team-05.answer: No: the projection is centrally symmetric, so it cannot be a pentagon.

hmmt-feb-2018-team-06.prompt: Let $n\ge2$ be a positive integer. A subset of positive integers $S$ is said to be *comprehensive* if for every integer $0\le x<n$, there is a subset of $S$ whose sum has remainder $x$ when divided by $n$. Note that the empty set has sum $0$. Show that if a set $S$ is comprehensive, then there is some (not necessarily proper) subset of $S$ with at most $n-1$ elements which is also comprehensive.
hmmt-feb-2018-team-06.answer: If $|S|\ge n$, some element can be removed without losing any remainder, by tracking the set of attainable remainders as elements are added.

hmmt-feb-2018-team-07.prompt: Let $[n]$ denote the set of integers $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$. We randomly choose a function $f:[n]\to[n]$, out of the $n^n$ possible functions. We also choose an integer $a$ uniformly at random from $[n]$. Find the probability that there exist positive integers $b,c\ge1$ such that $f^b(1)=a$ and $f^c(a)=1$. ($f^k(x)$ denotes the result of applying $f$ to $x$ $k$ times.)

hmmt-feb-2018-team-08a.prompt:
Allen plays a game on a tree with $2n$ vertices, each of whose vertices can be red or blue. Initially, all of the vertices of the tree are colored red. In one move, Allen is allowed to take two vertices of the same color which are connected by an edge and change both of them to the opposite color. He wins if at any time, all of the vertices of the tree are colored blue.

(A *graph* consists of a set of vertices and some edges between distinct pairs of vertices. It is *connected* if every pair of vertices are connected by some path of one or more edges. A *tree* is a graph which is connected, in which the number of edges is one less than the number of vertices.)

Show that Allen can win if and only if the vertices can be split up into two groups $V_1$ and $V_2$ of size $n$, such that each edge in the tree has one endpoint in $V_1$ and one endpoint in $V_2$.
hmmt-feb-2018-team-08a.answer: The unique bipartition of the tree must be balanced (invariant: blue count difference); conversely, induct by clearing two leaves along a path.

hmmt-feb-2018-team-08b.prompt:
Allen plays a game on a tree with $2n$ vertices, each of whose vertices can be red or blue. Initially, all of the vertices of the tree are colored red. In one move, Allen is allowed to take two vertices of the same color which are connected by an edge and change both of them to the opposite color. He wins if at any time, all of the vertices of the tree are colored blue.

(A *graph* consists of a set of vertices and some edges between distinct pairs of vertices. It is *connected* if every pair of vertices are connected by some path of one or more edges. A *tree* is a graph which is connected, in which the number of edges is one less than the number of vertices.)

Suppose Allen can win, and let $V_1=\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ and $V_2=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be the two groups from the characterization (every edge joins $V_1$ to $V_2$, $|V_1|=|V_2|=n$). Let $M$ be the minimum over all permutations $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ of the quantity $$\sum_{i=1}^nd(a_i,b_{\sigma(i)}),$$ where $d(v,w)$ denotes the number of edges along the shortest path between vertices $v$ and $w$ in the tree.

Show that if Allen can win, then the minimum number of moves that it can take for Allen to win is equal to $M$.
hmmt-feb-2018-team-08b.answer: Both quantities equal $M'=\sum_e d_e$, where $d_e$ is the imbalance $|{|C\cap V_1|-|C\cap V_2|}|$ of a component $C$ of $T-e$.

hmmt-feb-2018-team-09.prompt: Evan has a simple graph with $v$ vertices and $e$ edges. Show that he can delete at least $\frac{e-v+1}2$ edges so that each vertex still has at least half of its original degree.
hmmt-feb-2018-team-09.answer: Strong induction on $e$: delete every other edge of an even closed trail; if there is none, all cycles are odd and vertex-disjoint, so delete one edge per cycle.

hmmt-feb-2018-team-10.prompt:
Let $n$ and $m$ be positive integers which are at most $10^{10}$. Let $R$ be the rectangle with corners at $(0,0),(n,0),(n,m),(0,m)$ in the coordinate plane. A simple non-self-intersecting quadrilateral with vertices at integer coordinates is called *far-reaching* if each of its vertices lie on or inside $R$, but each side of $R$ contains at least one vertex of the quadrilateral. Show that there is a far-reaching quadrilateral with area at most $10^6$.

(A side of a rectangle includes the two endpoints.)
hmmt-feb-2018-team-10.answer: Two constructions: one of area $g=\gcd(n,m)$ (Pick) and one of area $\le\frac12\left(\frac ng+\frac mg\right)$; the smaller is at most $\sqrt{(n+m)/2}\le10^5$.
